summary.text: A female infant, a diamniotic monochorionic twin, was born by emergent caesarean section at 25 weeks and 2 days gestation for maternal pre-eclampsia with severe features. She was intubated at birth, managed with high-frequency oscillatory ventilation, received surfactant, parenteral nutrition with lipids via a central line and empiric ampicillin and gentamicin for 36 hours.

On day of life six a small right flank ecchymosis progressed over 6–12 hours to the entire back. She was emergently transferred to a level IV NICU for concern for possible invasive infection. A pre-transfer wound culture showed no organisms on Gram stain and no fungal growth. Labs showed WBC 21.1, platelets 146 and CRP 4.5. Broad spectrum antibiotics and liposomal amphotericin B were started after transfer, frozen section biopsy showed fungal elements concerning for Rhizopus and Aspergillus, and surgical debridement of the back was performed within 6 hours of transfer with four additional debridements on D1 and D2; antibiotics were stopped on D2.

Her status worsened with escalating sedation, pain control and vasoactive support, and micafungin was added on D4. On D6 fungal cultures grew Aspergillus flavus; species identification was subsequently confirmed by MALDI-TOF, prompting a switch to voriconazole. Head ultrasound on D6 showed a large right ACA infarction and by D8 progressive infarction with hemorrhagic transformation and midline shift, concerning for intracranial angioinvasive disease.

She transitioned to comfort care and passed on D10. Susceptibility results returned after her death showed an amphotericin B MIC of 4 μg/mL, with micafungin at or below 0.015, voriconazole 0.5, posaconazole 0.125, itraconazole 0.06 and isavuconazole 0.5 μg/mL. The mother's placenta was free of fungal elements; the twin, who had passed two days before D0 from pulmonary hemorrhage, had no evidence of fungal disease at autopsy. Her autopsy showed residual fungal involvement confined to the cutaneous wound sites without histopathological evidence of invasive aspergillosis in the brain.
